ratings.excerpt: Feat of spectacle and seduction … F Scott Fitzgerald’s classic story of dashed American dreams becomes an impressive, glitzy romcom musical … This musical based on F Scott Fitzgerald’s classic novel is a juggernaut of a show and as such it takes a while to get moving... For a few scenes it almost feels as if Marc Bruni’s production might stall. And then we meet Jay Gatsby (Jamie Muscato) and boy, are we rolling. … Visually, the show is stunning. Paul Tate DePoo III’s scenic and projection design is all sumptuous Roaring Twenties, meticulous in its detail. … Music, by Jason Howland, is more of a patchwork of styles. The stakes are high in the great Gatsby gamble — but does it pay off? … Stick with this musical makeover of F Scott Fitzgerald’s masterly novel — it’s worth the wait … ... at first sluggish, finally persuasive, always technically dazzling Broadway musical version … Yet excellent though the cast turn out to be, Marc Bruni’s production is the star here. … ... in a far superior second half. Suddenly the show clears more space for production numbers — great tap dancing included — and starts feeling like its own thing. … ... when McCann sings the song Beautiful Little Fool, she makes Daisy’s tunnel vision feel both vividly selfish and like necessary self-preservation. … Best of all is Muscato’s Gatsby. A little empty beneath the razzmattaz … The award-winning Broadway musical version of Fitzgerald’s novel hits London as a lavish spectacle but lacking heart … In performance this Gatsby turns out to be a sleek, ravishingly designed ocean liner of a show, with enough musical oomph and vocal power to distract you from the hollowness at its heart. … It’s staged with pizzaz by the original Broadway director/choreographer team of Marc Bruni and Dominique Kelley(YES). Strong performances from Frances Mayli McCann’s Daisy Buchanan and Amber Davies’s Jordan Baker make up for the insipidity of Jamie Muscato as the titular antihero and Corbin Bleu as our narrator, Nick Carraway. … Seldom has this plot, and Gatsby’s miraculous self-reinvention, seemed more fantastical. The Great Gatsby musical is vacuous - pretty costumes can't save it … It's lovely to look at, but those expecting a meaningful analysis of wealth and class are going to be disappointed … What it lacks (and it lacks a great deal) in meaningful exploration of the themes and ideas that have made this text a classic, it attempts to compensate for with bucketloads of Jazz Age razzle-dazzle. Dazzling, but not the greatest Gatsby … Verdict: A spectacle old sport … Marc Bruni's dazzling production of The Great Gatsby opened on Broadway last year and now – with a mostly British cast – bursts into life in the West End. But while the musical adaptation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's great American novel about money and class looks like a million dollars, the creators still struggle to overcome the essential problem of the work: none of the leading characters are likeable, not even narrator Nick Carraway (Corbin Bleu), who may not be nasty or vapid but is still (whisper it) a bit of a sap. … Muscato captures the character's cool detachment, and has a beautiful singing voice in a production that sounds terrific (even if the songs are as ephemeral as the green lamp at the end of Daisy's doc

Luxuriously glitzy yet glib West End musical … Despite hosting the British premieres of Broadway classics like Guys and Dolls and Kiss Me, Kate, the Coliseum sometimes feels too grandiose for musicals…but not for The Great Gatsby... a maximalist staging by Marc Bruni that demonstrates where every penny of your ticket money went. A crude, vulgar musical of Fitzgerald’s dark masterpiece … Like other interpretations before it, this take on the great Jazz Age novel pounces on the party vibe and misses almost everything else … A more ambitious creative team might have turned The Great Gatsby’s keening lyricism, elusive spirit and sheer tragic beauty to its advantage. Instead, we get a screechy clodhopping musical that amps up the Roaring Twenties clichés at the expense of anything Fitzgerald had to say about class, money and the scissoring chasms between appearances and reality. … ... Jamie Muscato, so brilliant in Natasha and Pierre and the Great Comet of 1812 at the Donmar, struggles to preserve Gatsby’s evasive, essentially unknowable soul. Big, brash, noisy and one-dimensional … F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Gatsby is little more than a loner with a taste for yearning power ballads and a spot of tap-dancing … There are two kinds of Great Gatsby fans. The first cherish F. Scott Fitzgerald’s tale as an exquisite meditation on the Jazz Age version of the American Dream. The others are more interested in dressing up in fancy threads and quaffing champagne at retro parties. The composer Jason Howland, lyricist Nathan Tysen and director Marc Bruni have brought a musical to the London Coliseum that is aimed very much at the latter. … Where the novel is concise, understated and allusive, this show — which opened on Broadway last year — is big, brash, noisy and oddly one-dimensional. Ludicrously lavish, The Great Gatsby musical lacks a basic level of respect for F Scott Fitzgerald’s original … As Gatsby, Jamie Muscato brings stupendous vocals and a jarringly approachable goofiness to the most elusive of literary creations … ... what Kait Kerrigan’s weirdly larky book and Marc Bruni’s ludicrously lavish production lack is a basic level of respect for F Scott Fitzgerald’s elegy for the Roaring Twenties, or an understanding of what makes it more than an excellent theme for a hen do. … ... What a swell party this ain’t … F Scott Fitzgerald’s classic jazz age novel ought to be the perfect basis for a musical, but no amount of Charlestons from a fine cast can put the fizz into this … There is a strong argument for turning F Scott Fitzgerald’s jazz-age critique of the American Dream into a musical, from the sound of the lavish parties at Jay Gatsby’s mansion to the natural lyricism in its prose. It does not transpose convincingly here, though not for the lack of size or volume. … Under the direction of Marc Bruni, it starts big, in sound and look...
